guides.explanation:
Velocity is a vector, so an object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating: its direction keeps changing. The acceleration points to the centre of the circle (centripetal means centre-seeking) and has magnitude $a_c = v^2/r$. If the speed is changing as well, there is also a tangential component, $a_t = dv/dt$, perpendicular to it.

Newton's second law then makes a demand: the net force toward the centre must equal $mv^2/r$. "Centripetal force" is not a new kind of force and never appears on a free-body diagram. It is a job done by real forces: tension for a ball on a string, static friction for a car on a flat bend, gravity for a satellite. Draw the real forces, take the direction toward the centre as positive, and set the sum of the inward components equal to $mv^2/r$.

At the top of the inside of a loop, gravity and the normal force both point toward the centre: $F_N + mg = mv^2/r$. The slowest possible speed there has $F_N = 0$, so $v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$. At the bottom, $F_N - mg = mv^2/r$, which is why you feel heavier there.

For a satellite in a circular orbit, gravity alone is the inward force: $GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r$. The satellite's mass cancels, leaving $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, and with $v = 2\pi r/T$ this becomes Kepler's third law, $T^2 = 4\pi^2r^3/(GM)$.

guides.derivation:
**Centripetal acceleration by differentiating.** An object moves at constant speed $v$ round a circle of radius $r$ centred on the origin. Let $\omega = v/r$ be the constant rate at which its angle increases so that the angle at time $t$ is $\omega t$ and the position is

$$
\vec{r}(t) = r\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{\imath} + r\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{\jmath}.
$$

Differentiate once to get the velocity:

$$
\vec{v}(t) = -r\omega\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{\imath} + r\omega\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{\jmath}.
$$

Its magnitude is $r\omega = v$, constant as assumed. Differentiate again:

$$
\vec{a}(t) = -r\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{\imath} - r\omega^2\sin(\omega t)\,\hat{\jmath} = -\omega^2\,\vec{r}(t).
$$

The acceleration is a negative multiple of the position vector, so it points from the object straight back to the centre. Its magnitude is

$$
a_c = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r}.
$$

This is pure kinematics: any object moving this way has this acceleration, whatever forces cause it.

**Circular orbits.** Set gravity equal to the required inward force, $GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r$, so that $v^2 = GM/r$. One orbit covers the circumference in one period, $v = 2\pi r/T$. Substituting,

$$
\frac{4\pi^2r^2}{T^2} = \frac{GM}{r} \quad\Rightarrow\quad T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}\,r^3.
$$

workedExamples.title: A car at the crest of a hill
workedExamples.prompt: A $1200\ \text{kg}$ car drives over the top of a hill whose crest is an arc of a vertical circle of radius $45\ \text{m}$. At the crest the car's speed is $15\ \text{m/s}$. Find the normal force the road exerts on the car there, and the greatest speed at which the car can cross the crest without leaving the road. Use $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
steps: The centre of the circle is below the car, inside the hill, so at the crest "toward the centre" means downward. The weight $mg$ points inward and the normal force $F_N$ outward.
Inward sum: $mg - F_N = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.
The road cannot pull the car down, so the limit is $F_N = 0$, where gravity alone supplies the inward force: $v_{\max} = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{(9.8)(45)} = 21\ \text{m/s}$.
workedExamples.answer: $F_N = 5.8 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N}$, upward; above $21\ \text{m/s}$ the car leaves the road

workedExamples.title: A conical pendulum
workedExamples.prompt: A $0.20\ \text{kg}$ ball on a light string of length $1.2\ \text{m}$ moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle, with the string making a constant angle of $30^\circ$ with the vertical. Determine the tension in the string, the speed of the ball and the period of its motion. Use $g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
steps: Two forces act on the ball: its weight $mg$ and the tension $F_T$ along the string. Nothing pushes outward. The acceleration is horizontal, toward the centre of the circle, of radius $r = L\sin\theta = (1.2)(\sin 30^\circ) = 0.60\ \text{m}$.
Vertical direction (no acceleration): $F_T\cos\theta - mg = 0$, so $F_T = \dfrac{(0.20)(9.8)}{\cos 30^\circ} = 2.3\ \text{N}$.

Horizontal direction (toward the centre): $F_T\sin\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. Dividing this by the vertical equation, $F_T\cos\theta = mg$, gives $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$, so $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta} = \sqrt{(0.60)(9.8)(0.577)} = 1.84\ \text{m/s}$.
Period: $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi(0.60)}{1.84} = 2.0\ \text{s}$.
workedExamples.answer: $F_T = 2.3\ \text{N}$, $v = 1.8\ \text{m/s}$ and $T = 2.0\ \text{s}$

misconceptions.wrong: An object moving in a circle is pushed outward by a centrifugal force that balances the inward force.
misconceptions.right: In an inertial frame there is no outward force, and the forces do not balance: if they did, the object would move in a straight line. The outward feeling in a turning car is your body's tendency to carry straight on.

misconceptions.wrong: The centripetal force is an extra force to draw on the free-body diagram, alongside tension, gravity and friction.
misconceptions.right: It is the name for the net inward result of those real forces. Draw only forces that some object exerts, then set their inward sum equal to $mv^2/r$.

misconceptions.wrong: At constant speed there is no acceleration, so no net force is needed to go round a circle.
misconceptions.right: Constant speed is not constant velocity. The direction of the velocity keeps changing, which is an acceleration of $v^2/r$ toward the centre.

checkYourself.q: A car rounds a flat bend of radius $50\ \text{m}$ at a steady $10\ \text{m/s}$. What is its acceleration, and which force provides it?
checkYourself.a: $a_c = v^2/r = 2\ \text{m/s}^2$, toward the centre of the bend, provided by static friction from the road.

checkYourself.q: The same car takes the same bend at twice the speed. How does the friction force needed change?
checkYourself.a: Four times as large: the required inward force $mv^2/r$ depends on the square of the speed.

checkYourself.q: A coin sits on a turntable turning at a steady rate. Which force keeps the coin moving in a circle, and what happens if the turntable gradually speeds up?
checkYourself.a: Static friction, pointing toward the centre. The inward force needed, $mv^2/r$, grows with the speed; once it exceeds the most that static friction can supply, the coin slides off.

guides.teacherNotes: Ban the phrase "centripetal force" from free-body diagrams: every arrow must have an agent, and $mv^2/r$ goes on the other side of the equation. Ask students to mark the centre of the circle and the inward direction before writing anything; most sign errors at the top of loops and hills come from skipping this. The car-on-a-crest and inside-of-a-loop cases make a good pair, because the normal force points away from the centre in one and toward it in the other.
